cultivar: Wuyi cai cha (local small-leaf population bushes)
processing: Fully oxidised, unsmoked Tongmu black from a bud with one or two young leaves (Da Chi Gan takes two or three): withered, rolled, oxidised and dried at low heat.
harvest_season: Spring, from late April into May, picked after the bud teas; one harvest a year in the reserve.
appearance_dry: Small, tight, slightly curly dark strands with reddish stems and a few bronze tips.
appearance_wet: Small copper leaves with reddish stalks, whole and even.
taste_profile: Honey and dried longan over cocoa and sweet potato, with more body and grip than the bud teas and the same cool, clean Tongmu finish.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan, water near the boil, no rinse, short steeps; the extra leaf makes it forgiving of long steeps. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, usually released from early summer after a short rest; drinks well for two or three years and is often better in its second year. Lao cong (old-bush) Chi Gan is sold with the year and bush age stated.
description:
Xiao Chi Gan is the everyday black tea of Tongmu, the Wuyi village that gave the world Lapsang souchong and Jin Jun Mei. The name means something like 'small red-sweet', after the reddish stems of the picked shoot, and it marks a picking standard: a bud with one or two young leaves. Da Chi Gan, 'big red-sweet', is a bud with two or three. Together they are what Tongmu makers drink themselves, and what most of the village's bushes actually go into.

The leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried without smoke, just like unsmoked Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong; in practice the names overlap, and Chi Gan is best thought of as the finer-picked end of the unsmoked Tongmu range, below Yin Jun Mei and above standard Xiao Zhong. It briefly carried the name Tong Jun Mei ('copper eyebrow') when the Jun Mei family was launched, which tells you where it sits.

In the cup it is honey and dried longan over cocoa and sweet potato, with a bit more body and grip than the bud teas and that cool, clean finish Tongmu teas share. It is sturdy: water near the boil, no rinse, short steeps, eight or more infusions, and it shrugs off a forgotten steep. Lao cong lots from old bushes add a mossy, woody depth and a longer finish.

It is sold by the current spring harvest from named villages inside the reserve, at a fraction of Jin Jun Mei prices, and it is the Tongmu tea least worth faking, which makes it the safest buy from a seller you do not know. Check that the leaf is small and even with reddish stalks; big, flat leaf with golden fuzz is from somewhere else.

If you want to understand what 'Tongmu character' means without spending Jin Jun Mei money, this is the tea to buy.
sources_note: Naming conventions (Xiao/Da Chi Gan, Tong Jun Mei) follow Tongmu makers' usage and vary between sellers.
